utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case please, Mr. Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-02-60-T, the Prosecutor versus Vidoje Blagojevic and Dragan Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Mr. Karnavas, are there any protective measures for the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: None were sought, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I see. So could we have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. I can't hear you. Maybe there's a technical problem.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration in accordance with the paper the usher is showing to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down, please. Well, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Judge Vassylenko.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Good morning, sir. I understand you speak English but you will be speaking in your native tongue, Dutch. Is that right. If you could please tell us your name.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: My name is Thomas Jakob Peter Karremans.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Could you please spell your last name for the record.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: K-a-r-r-e-m-a-n-s.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karremans, if we could -- first I want to concentrate on your background, so I will ask you a few questions. Could you please tell us a little bit about yourself, where you're from, what line of work have you been in.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: I was born in 1948, in Appledorn in the Netherlands. I attended secondary school. I did my required military service in Seedorf, Germany. In 1970, I entered the royal military academy in Breda. I subsequently completed a programme to serve as an officer in the infantry, and then I successively proceeded through military ranks and functions that are standard for somebody who has graduated from the royal military academy, including programmes, courses, and so on. I was in the first deployment of UNIFIL in Lebanon as a COI commander. I served two functions in the Belgian NATO headquarters. I was subsequently head of the department arms inspections and spent a lot of time in former Warsaw Pact countries. And afterwards I was assigned to an infantry battalion in Assen which was transferred into the air mobile command, where as a commander of DutchBat 3, I went to Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But I take it your career did not end - your military career, that is - after you left Bosnia. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: Following my return from Bosnia, I basically had to overhaul the battalion in Assen because many of the higher-ranking staff were transferred elsewhere. Afterwards, I went on several practice sessions with the battalion and transferred the battalion in 1996. We prepared for being stationed in the United States. I spent three years working in the United States. From the United States, I went to Heidelberg where I spent three years as the head of operations at NATO headquarters. And from Heidelberg, I went to Madrid where I served as the head of personnel and logistic affairs at NATO headquarters. And from Madrid last October I retired, which is called functional age dismissal. That's the way the Dutch terminology is for retiring.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Witness, I understand that you're eager to give your evidence, but you have to understand whatever you say has to be translated from Dutch to English so that we could catch up with you. So please make a pause after every sentence, or the counsel will lead you step by step.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In English] Okay. Understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, for that intervention. I was just about to mention that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, before we get more into the substance of today's testimony, if you could tell us first how many times you've given testimony with respect to the events concerning Srebrenica; how many times, where, when, so at least we have a record of that.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: That depends on the context of your question. Do you mean a commission or a small committee? Or do you mean an officially appointed investigation body?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I mean everything.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: Do you mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Everything.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: I did not keep track of how often, but generally I was debriefed on a few occasions, several occasions in fact. This began in Zagreb following my return from Srebrenica; once prior to the battalion going on leave, then the investigation in Assen where some members of the battalion were interrogated more times than other members. Some members were interrogated several times. I probably missed a few in between. Then of course there's the investigation by the state institute for war documentation which changed from the RIOD to the NIOD. I was sent from the United States to the Netherlands a few times for two- to three-day sessions of interrogation. Then I did an interview over the phone with Mr. Von Kemena. I was sent to the investigation in Paris by the Assen Bay for an investigation there. The preliminary discussions meant that I appeared for the Bakker commission, that was a parliamentary inquiry. And I forgot to mention the first one. Immediately after my arrival in the United States, I had to return to the Netherlands to appear before this institute; that was in 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, yesterday we had a chance to meet for the first time. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And we had what we call a rather brief conversation lasting about 30 minutes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Your microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Can I be heard now? No. It's on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Can I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: But I didn't see the light there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I don't see it either, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So long as it's working, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So yesterday we spoke for about 30 minutes, 30 to 45 minutes; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And during that period of time, you indicated that all of your testimonies and all of the transcripts you had available. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And it was your impression that all of this was also made available to the Office of the Prosecution. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: I assumed that, because most of the documents compiled during the interrogations and hearings and conversations are public, in my view, in the sense that the examining magistrate or judicial institution would have access to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And I understand you also wrote a book about your experience in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And in reading your book, it would appear that you had also made references to another book written about Srebrenica called Endgame by a David Rohde. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: Yes. I refer to two books, one by Rohde and the other title escapes me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: By Dutch authors, the other book? Okay. Very well. Let's talk about your mission to Srebrenica. First of all, could you please tell us what sort of a debriefing -- or briefing, I should say, you received prior to going to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: In preparation for my deployment, as is standard procedure, there were many activities which, as I mentioned, follow a standard protocol. I can put it that way. They need to be done so that a unit where people receive individual as well as group training for their deployment in a relatively short period. They need to be made ready to start the mission. Part of this preparation comprises briefings, briefings about staff, about the situation, documents about culture, history, you name it. We received debriefings during our preparation period in Assen. We received some documents to read about services that gathered information, that might be useful prior to enduring the deployment mission. We learned about the ongoing operations of the battalion stationed in that area, so we were in contact with people in the unit who were there at that point. And I spent a week in that area with some officers prior to our deployment there. During that week, everybody operates as -- with his counterpart, so a peace commander visits the peace commander who is -- who he will be replacing. A staff officer speaks with his counterpart, the official whose duties he will be taking over when his mission starts. And I spent a week with Colonel Everts. I spoke with him and he showed me a lot, the way he works, the way he worked, how the battalion worked, and he showed me the lay of the land. And he told me how the operations should proceed, and that was how we were prepared, if that's what you mean by briefings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Now, if we could go into a little more detail. You indicated that you learned about the situation and the ongoing operations. Could you please tell us whether you were informed about the activities of the Muslim army that was operating within the Srebrenica area.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: Yes, especially during my preliminary visit, the week that I spent there. I spoke with the information officer of the battalion and of course with the battalion commander as well about what was going on at that time. I believe I remember meeting several people in that area, tangentially speaking. And they informed me about the current state of affairs, that is to say both sides explained the situation. Imagine -- it follows we knew something and we received quite a bit of information already, but we received the best information on site from the -- from our predecessors. That's how the information exchange was organised. So what you're referring to regarding Bosnian Serbs and Muslims as well, in part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I take it then that your predecessor, Colonel Everts, would have received a similar briefing from his predecessor; correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And then of course the predecessor of Colonel Everts, which would have been DutchBat I, would have received a briefing from the Canadian Battalion; correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: I can't say. I wasn't there, but I assume so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And I take it before going is there, you yourself had an opportunity to read the UN resolutions establishing the enclave.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, did you have an opportunity to meet Naser Oric when you went there for that one-week orientation?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: I can't really say. I thought about who I met during that week. One week is not a very long time. I was inundated with impressions. I spent most of the day on my feet, and in response to another question you asked me I said I met a few people during that week. Whether Naser Oric was among them, I tend to think so but only very briefly. Because -- as I said, in passing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, did you meet with any of the Muslim commanders? Because I understand there were quite an if you of them running their own little fiefdoms within the enclave.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: One or two, but also, only in passing. We were introduced and then we just drove on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Were you introduced to any of the Serb counterparts from the VRS?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: No. I believe I was introduced to several people in the -- during the days I arrived in January, so during the transfer period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That was the actual period when you got there and they had that big banquet which lasted about eight hours. And I understand General Zivanovic spoke about seven of the eight hours.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: No, not during the period when I was taking over there. That must have happened during a different period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Now, did you by any chance have a visit of the collection point where the arms were being stored? And I'm speaking about the week that you went there.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, there was a collection point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And in listening to your background, you had worked in the department of arms inspection. And I take it you had a familiarity with the weapons that you were able to see at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You didn't recognise the weapons, what they were, the capabilities?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: In my function as the head of the arms inspections department of the army staff, I was involved with implementing a policy based on the CSE treaty. The treaty was signed in Paris by NATO on the one hand, the Warsaw Pact on the other hand, and each country had an organisation to inspect that was agreed in that treaty. That's what we meant by arms inspections. And in that capacity, I visited the former Warsaw Pact countries on a few occasions. That's not the same thing as when you see a few weapons at a weapon collection point which were, in fact, well-maintained of all kinds of makes and brands.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But nonetheless part of your mandate was to implement a policy sell up by the UN for a demilitarisation process within the enclave which would require by its very nature some sort of arms inspection, would it not?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Did you recognise the arms when you saw them? Do you know --

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: I recognised some of them by type, and I'm referring to the more sophisticated weapons at the collection point. But there were also weapons that looked almost like they had been put together manually. They were really very simple. It was quite ingenious the way they thought about it. They were obviously not from some munitions factory but had been thrown together in a shed somewhere. So there was a wide variety in terms of weapons at the collection point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Do you know whether when you went back to actually take your position, the amount of weapons had increased or decreased in that collection point?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: Increased, but in a limited measure in the sense that I spoke to Colonel Everts about this explicitly and we agreed that it wasn't always easy in the context of demilitarisation to seize weapons from armed Muslim groups if there were large numbers of them. You can disarm an individual; that's not so difficult. But at the end of our period I noticed that there were units there - but I assume we'll get into that in more detail later on - there were units that were fully armed. And in that case, disarming such units is far more complicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. I take it Colonel Everts had impressed upon you the challenges that he had met during the week that you were there.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Could I ask you: What, if anything, did you do when you came back to meet with your superiors, at least to alert them as to the challenges that awaited you, the challenges, that is, that Colonel Everts was having a rather difficult time, I would suspect, in overcoming?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understood the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, before going there you knew that the place had to be demilitarised. Colonel Everts obviously informed you about the challenges that he had met in this process. When you came back to meet with your superiors, did you alert them that challenges awaited for you with respect to this -- with respect to the demilitarisation aspect in order to perhaps have your superiors assist you in some way to meet the upcoming challenges?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: No. It's only possible to do that by telephone because of the location -- or I should say the dislocation of the safe area. And considering the structure at the time between the battalion and the higher echelons, the fact that when you're talking about superiors we were not in contact with the members of the higher echelons daily or weekly, monthly, which is normal in UN operations. And this is what the commander of DutchBat I had to do and the commander of DutchBat II and I, too. It was basically like reinventing the wheel as far as disclosing something or contributing something to negotiations and trying to make clear what our intentions were based on what we were assigned by the United Nations and I assume disclosed to both parties. So communication was one of the main problems, one of the biggest problems. And talking to superiors about demilitarisation was, at best, going through reports that were issued daily or weekly through assessments.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, actually you anticipated my next line of questioning. But first what I'm interested in: You were in the field, you spent the week in the field, you got debriefed in the field, then you came back to the Netherlands before you and your battalion were to go off to Srebrenica. So my question is: When you came back after having that whole week in situ, as they say, getting an assessment, did you at that time, before heading off with your men, did you contact your superiors to inform them that perhaps part of the mission was going to be very difficult to meet in light of the challenges that Colonel Everts had informed you of and in light of your own observations and assessments?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: Yes, because after a reconnaissance mission we draft a report with some annexes, and the annexes are the individual reports of all members of the team. And we have a few conclusions and recommendations attached to that. That's the report that we send to our boss, the upper echelon. But at this time, I'm not sure whether one of the issues, that's demilitarisation, I'm not sure whether that appeared in the report, but I assume it did because that was a very tough issue. But the Netherlands, or rather, our Dutch boss, when we were involved in the preparations can't really help that because it's an UN affair. And we need to mention that to the UN channels. And that means that the commander of DutchBat I and DutchBat II and then subsequently I myself reported in writing through faxes. And as I just said, assess reps and the like, as to whether things are working out or not and whether we can comply with demilitarisation and how it's progressing and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, if you could please tell us what the goals of the mission were. Perhaps we can start there and take it.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: Well, that forces me to go back in my memory. When I think back, I remember what the afternoon objectives were, and they were to provide protection under the UN to the population within the Srebrenica safe area. The UNHR and other NGOs, we were expected to assist them so that they could perform their duties there. Third, we were expected to help the population, which was the main purpose at the end of the day, and we received certain means to help the population. I believe that demilitarisation is part of the primary task.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, first I wanted to go to your statement -- or the testimony, I should say, that you gave to this Tribunal back in 1996 when things were slightly fresher in your mind, I suspect, since it was 1996. And at that point in time - I don't know if you've had a chance to look at your statement, but I'll just read a portion of it and perhaps we can talk about that a little bit. You were asked on page 603, and at that particular hearing which took place on 3 July 1996, it was the Mladic/Karadzic hearing, Rule 62 hearing, you were asked about your mission and you said that on page 603: "I can expand on that, but I have first, let us say, to explain what the mission was of the battalion." And Mr. Harmon from the Office of the Prosecution who is still with us in this building who was questioning you. He says: "Please." Go ahead, in other words. And your answer was: "That was twofold. One was the purely military side of the mission and the other side was the humanitarian one." And I'm reading from lines 4 onwards, incidentally. And then you go on to say: "The military side was to look to the cease-fire agreement between both warring factions of both parties to assist the civil authorities in the opstina of Srebrenica to maintain negotiations between the BSA and the BiH and of course trying to reject the BSA from attacking the enclave. On the other hand, the humanitarian side of the mission was to support the refugees within the enclave as much as possible on medical by food, by let us say the infrastructure within the enclave to enhance that, and that was, let us say, the second part of the mission of the battalion." So it would appear back in 1996, July 3rd - and perhaps it was out of nervousness or a failure of memory at that point in time - that you didn't see or at least you didn't testify to the demilitarisation as being one of the parts of the mission.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: No, and I don't have to. If the question isn't put to me, I don't have to answer it. I don't need to explain that the execution of a military mission comprises more than just what may be written on paper. And that is linked with the execution of the activities in terms of intelligence, or how you can still perform a military action in a better way when you can prepare it in a military way. When you refer to demilitarisation, then that is only a small part of what needs to be done. I'm not sure if this is an issue which I forgot about at the time or whether I included it in my listing now because you have been referring to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, if I could just put this on the ELMO, just this page. I just want to make sure that I'm fair with you, sir, because it is you on page 603, line 1, that state that you want to explain what the mission was of the battalion. And then you say "two-fold." Now, on the purely military side of the mission, there's nothing about - if we go on and we look at it, you say it was: "To look to the cease-fire agreement," and that's different than demilitarisation because you can hold a cease-fire and demilitarisation. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: That's the why you should view it, I think; it's part of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's the way we should view it. Okay. But they're not mutually exclusive. I guess that's what I'm asking. In other words, you can have a cease-fire or say when you were the -- implementing the arms inspection, as you know there was an arms buildup between the United States and Russia. They were still -- they were not at war with each other but they were still arm-building. Right?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: No. That's an entirely different issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I was using that by way of analogy, that you can have a cease-fire and still militarise at the same time. Okay. And then you go on to say that: "To assist the civil authorities in the opstina of Srebrenica," -- okay, nothing about demilitarisation there -- "to maintain negotiations between the BSA and the BiH and, of course, trying to reject the BSA from attacking the enclave." So it would appear, sir, that at least when you testified you failed to mention anything about demilitarisation at that aspect of your testimony, right there?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: Because, as you have just been saying, demilitarisation is only part of the military side of the mission. Intelligence is another part which I didn't mention. And bringing parties together to negotiate when something had happened is part of that side of the mission. And that, too, wasn't mentioned in here. Then I was asked what did the mission consist of; I said two-fold, one humanitarian, second military.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And if I understand your testimony, as far as you were concerned the demilitarisation was a minor or small part of the overall mission.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: Minor but important.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. Okay. Well, I just wanted to refresh your memory perhaps with a debriefing report. Perhaps you can comment on that. This is a report, the Assen report, 4 October 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I can get the assistance of Mr. Usher and perhaps we can put page 8 on the ELMO. And if we could -- all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now. I just want to look where we see the section on mandate. Page 8, paragraph 2.20. If we go towards the middle of it, it says: "The most important aspect of this agreement was the demilitarisation of the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves. It was intended that all military or paramilitary units would either withdraw from the demilitarised zone or surrender all their arms and all ammunitions, mines, and explosives to UNPROFOR. Furthermore, UNPROFOR would now be authorised to confiscate arms and ammunition in the possession of civilians. UNPROFOR would also be given complete freedom of movement to and from the enclave." Now, just if you could help us out here, Mr. Karremans. Would you agree with this part of the debriefing report, that is, the most important aspect of the agreement that had been reached back in April 1993 between the two sides was the full and complete and continuous demilitarisation of the enclave?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: I don't see it here in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, maybe I can -- we can go to it. Again, I'm referring --

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: I see a section concerning the mandate, that is 2.20, dating from April 1993. "The enclave was under threat of," et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And incidentally I'm referring to what has come into evidence as P851. Well, let me ask you: Is it your opinion that your mandate changed? The mandate that you had back in 1995 was different from the mandate back in 1993, that is for the complete and continuous demilitarisation of the enclave itself?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: No, it was not changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: During 1993 to 1995. Only -- I told you that in order to implement it, that that wasn't always very easy, and that it was part of our military mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand that. And I guess I just want to make sure that I understand that you understood that that was the most important aspect of the agreement, the demilitarisation process. Would you agree with this report, or do you think --

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: No, I don't agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough. Now, when you came back for that week -- from the week of spending in the field, was it your opinion that you could not achieve that aspect of your mandate, that you would not have been able under any circumstances to demilitarise the Muslim army within the enclave?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: Well, it was possible. And, actually, it was executed by my two predecessors, the two commanders, whenever someone or a group of people walked around openly carrying arms. What I explained before is that in a later period, this was no longer possible. There were moments or prolonged periods - I mean days, sometimes a week or two weeks - when shots were fired from or in or around the enclave. But you never saw anyone walking around with arms, whereas we knew that there were people who possessed arms. We were not allowed to order homes to be searched. In other words, one could only seize a weapon in accordance with a standing procedure, when indeed you found someone having such a weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: In the course of my stay with DutchBat III, this became somewhat more difficult, because the number of people having arms in uniform increased. You can try, if you like, but with a patrol of three or four people you cannot disarm a group of 30 or 40.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, getting back -- if I can dissect this answer of yours. You said that it was possible to demilitarise. If that were the case, do you have an explanation as to why Colonel Everts, DutchBat II or DutchBat I or the Canadian DutchBat [sic], or all three of them together could not demilitarise this rather small enclave prior to your arrival, keeping in mind they had a couple of years?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: I didn't say it was possible to demilitarise an enclave. I said that on the basis of the experience of both my predecessors and our own experience, it was very difficult to seize all arms that were there, because apparently people did not comply with what was contained in the agreement about demilitarisation. I also explained that from time to time it worked, because you never saw anyone walking around with arms because we raised the issue during talks. And we regularly said that they should be handed over, which wasn't done by the way, until we found someone again, and then the procedure of seizure of arms was started.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: Or for a number of people. I want to add one thing. Considering and knowing the area, it is impossible geographically to disarm a population, or whatever you want to call it, because there are so many possibilities of hiding arms. And we cannot compare the area to a Dutch polder.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let me -- I just want to make sure that I understand your testimony. So while you were there you never saw anyone running around with arms? You didn't see any armed Muslim men in the streets all the way to the fall of Srebrenica? Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: No. That is not my testimony. My testimony is that we regularly stopped people with arms, but it varied. Sometimes we arrested one or two in a week, then things were quiet for a week or two. After that, the number was a little greater. Things varied and sometimes the men were capable of fleeing, leaving their arms behind or with their arms, depending on the current situation. But it was found -- it was seen, numbers have been seized. The weapons collection point grew, but not in the sense as we thought it should have grown.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, you said it was impossible to demilitarise this enclave. That's your testimony. Right?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: That is my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: That is also the statement of my two predecessors.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. That -- I was going to get to that. So in other words your predecessors knew that impossible to carry out one of the aspects of the agreement, the demilitarisation. Did you become aware that when you were there during that one week, or was it after you got into the field and actually started working in and around Srebrenica that you realised that this was mission impossible?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: I realised it, but not in the sense of a mission impossible. But I realised that it would become very difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, there's a difference between difficulty and impossibility. Would you agree with me on that?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: Difficult, yes, I agree. Difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So do you want to change your testimony to that you thought it was difficult or do you still think it was impossible? I'm just trying -- I'm not trying to pin you down but I'm trying to figure out so we can agree to set terms.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: Don't try to corner we with words, difficult or impossible. It was difficult. And concerning the circumstances and the means, the mandate, and the possibilities, as I just pointed out, we were not allowed to search homes and that sort of thing, it was nigh impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, in your estimation, were you able to at least be somewhat successful - perhaps not completely but somewhat successful - in carrying out the demilitarisation aspect of your mission?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And how successful? I mean, if you were going to grade yourself, how successful would you say you were?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: That's impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: And the reason why is that in the early period it could possibly have been done, but as time went by and as we saw, as I have stated before, that more as more people started run around with arms and also in uniforms, then at that time one would have to pass from a sufficient mark to an insufficient mark.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Would you say that the demilitarised zone, this enclave, had been more militarised during your -- during DutchBat III or demilitarised. Which of the two?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, were there more arms -- let me put it that way, a more simpler way of putting it. Were there more arms in the enclave by the time DutchBat III ended its mission or Srebrenica fell, or were there fewer on account of your, by your terms, modest successes in the demilitarisation process?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: More.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So not only were you not able to demilitarise, you were there -- or while you were there, the enclave was becoming more militarised.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, I just want to read a passage to you from a book, the Endgame. I can have it for the ELMO. I just want to get your opinion on whether you agree or disagree with this passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll be referring to page -- we need to get an -- give this an identification number. D208. And if we could just turn to page 164, 165. It's --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm getting a little ahead of my direct, but maybe since we're here on this issue you can help us out. Starting on the paragraph, the last -- the second-to-last paragraph. This is on July 11th, 1995. The second-to-last paragraph talks about a meeting that took place between General Delic and others. Apparently there was President Izetbegovic over there and Silajdzic. If we go to the very last paragraph, it says: "Without explaining why the army had pulled out Naser Oric and the enclave's fifteen best officers, he" -- being Delic -- "warned that there was no one strong enough in Srebrenica to create 'cohesion in the resistance.' 'Srebrenica at enough arms," he said. 'The only problem is how to create resistance.' The general pointed out that the army had 'made sure over the last few months' that more arms and ammunitions were in Srebrenica than there had been in three years. He mentioned the Chinese-made Red Arrow anti-tank missiles. 'Four tanks mean nothing,' Delic said, referring to the attack from the south. 'If a launcher with enough missiles is present.'" My question, Mr. Karremans, is: Would you agree with what General Delic of the Bosnian Muslim army at the time was saying, that is: While you were there, DutchBat III, Srebrenica had more arms and ammunitions than it had in the previous three years? Including these Chinese-made red arrow anti-tank missiles.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just to make sure that we all understand, that's a quote in a book. We don't know whether General Delic in fact said that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So it's entirely made clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm just wondering whether you agree with -- assuming that General Delic made this statement, and we have some footnotes to this passage - could you please tell us whether in your opinion General Delic was correct.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: I think every author of a book has the right to write whatever they like. I can give you no statement on this. I wasn't present at those talks. I don't know the man. I don't know how it ended up in this book. So I cannot give you a judgement. So my answer is: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But you were present in Srebrenica. And my question is: Would you say that in Srebrenica the Muslim army had the sort of weapons that are being mentioned by General Delic?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: No. I don't know that either, because those arms were not seized over the last period before the enclave was taken over because two large groups were running around with arms. So what type of arms is concerned is something I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, perhaps that might be a good time, Your Honour, to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, yes. Mr. Karnavas, I think we spent one sitting on the issue of demilitarisation. And it is an important issue in the Srebrenica incidents during that period, but I don't think first it is very relevant to our case. Secondly, I would like to say that this issue has been brought up many times before, and I don't think there are significant disputes between the parties. So my advice is that could we get over this part as soon as possible and come to the specific incidents this witness is an eyewitness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm laying the groundwork. I know the parties are rather close, but I wouldn't say that close. If we look at the -- that is the Prosecution and Defence on these issues, and because of the way the indictment is drafted I have to cover these points. I will move on as quickly as I can. I don't have much more on this issue, but we will be moving at a rather faster clip. But I'm also keeping in mind yesterday's comments on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And we'll have a break and we'll resume at quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Karremans, I want to turn to a section of your testimony at the Rule 61 hearing back on 4 July 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Perhaps we can have the assistance of the usher just to -- I guess we lost our usher. He will be coming back. Welcome. If you could put this on the ELMO. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, you were explaining - and I'm just going to go into this a little bit - you were talking about the challenges. And I'll be reading basically from -- picking up more or less where we had left off. You talked about the military aspect, the civilian -- the humanitarian side. And then you go on starting with line 15: "When we took over in January 1995 from, let us say, the 2nd Battalion, we were the third there, we had no problems during the rotation. We had no problems in the beginning with the BSA." That would be the Bosnian Serb army. Then you go on to say: "There were some problems with the BiH, the Bosnian forces, in the enclave." And of course that's the end of your answer. And the next question by Mr. Harmon from the Office of the Prosecution goes on: "What problems developed with the Bosnian Serb military?" So in light of the fact that they didn't give you an opportunity to explain what sort of problems you had with the BiH forces, I thought I might give you that opportunity right now, some several years later, to tell us.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: Communication was the problem, both ways. We found it easier to communicate with the people of the BiH, because they were represented in the enclave. And we devised a system of communicating with them. My Section 5 ordinarily did that, including -- which included Vujadin and two others who conducted and attended the weekly meetings. If a logistic problem arose in the enclave and needed to be discussed, then my deputy Franken usually did that or I sat in. If a serious problem arose in the sense of problems we perceived in the enclave as a whole, then I was the one who conducted the discussions. We never really had trouble conducting discussions and communicating with the BiH. On the other hand, some problems did arise with respect to communicating with representatives of the BSA. The discussions always took place on the border or just over the border of the enclave, often at a post that we called Jovo. That was where you entered the enclave. Any agreements reached with one of the BSA members always involved waiting to see if they were there. We never had an agenda.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I could interrupt you here for a second. The question was -- you said earlier back then in 1996 on July 4th that: "There were some problems with the BiH, the Bosnian forces, in the enclave." And today you said there were communication problems perhaps. And I noticed that nowhere in your testimony were you either asked by Mr. Harmon or did you volunteer any information with respect to the incident in the Bandera triangle or what was known as the Bandera triangle. My question is: Is that what you were referring to back when you said: "There were some problems with the BiH forces"?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: Among others.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Is there a particular reason why that escaped you from mentioning it back in July 4th, 1996, when you were testifying on behalf of the Prosecution against General Mladic and President Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: I assume you know that there were many problems, and the Bandera triangle was only one of the problems. And the fact that the battalion did not have freedom of action within the Srebrenica enclave to move about on foot or in vehicles because parts or off-limits to us was a problem that we discussed extensively with the BiH during the early period. As I described in my book, several men were held hostage for a period; that was a problem. And the problem concerning the arms that we discussed earlier was also a problem. Later on it was noted that increasing numbers of men were wearing new uniforms; that was a problem. Communication was not actually a problem. And sometimes communication was complicated, but it was generally rather smooth. With the BSA, on the other hand, that was a different situation. There was a communication problem there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. We're going to get to that; trust me. But I want to stick with what was happening on the enclave. Now, going back to what I had read earlier, the mandate which you said hadn't changed, included the complete freedom of movement within the enclave by UNPROFOR. And now you just told us that there were some parts that you did not have access to. Question: Were you aware of that before you went to Srebrenica or is that something that was unique to DutchBat III?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: That was unique for DutchBat III.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. As I understand it - and I don't want to be leading you too much on this, but I'm trying to speed up the process a bit - as I understand it, some 100 of your men were held hostage by the Muslim forces that were supposed to have been demilitarised. The same people that you were supposed to protect were actually holding you -- your men hostage. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Could you please tell us, so we have a clear record, why were the UN forces there being held hostage? By whom? For how long? And how did the hostage situation, this crisis, if I may call it that, was resolved.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: As you rightly observed, under the mandate an UN unit in a specific area was supposed to have all possible freedom of movement to perform its duties. Part of the area was -- we were denied access to; we called that the Bandera triangle. During a period when the weather conditions were atrocious, because we anticipated potential problems within the area, we wanted to set up an old existing recon post where the local officer in command - if that's what you would like to call him - was -- he did not like this and he did not allow us to do that. In other words, an UN unit, DutchBat III, did not have complete freedom of movement within its own area. Obviously, I communicated this to my superiors in several telephone calls and reports I told Brussels about this and to break the impasse I conducted a few meetings with Naser Oric. And ultimately through mediation from higher up, negotiations, discussions at higher levels, after a number of days the hostages were released.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. How many days were your men held hostage?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: Two or three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And who did you have to communicate up the ladder to, so we know how high this negotiating process had to go to so at least to get your men released from the Muslim army inside the enclave?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: For the record and for your personal information - I don't know whether I still need to explain this - my point of contact, my commander was in Tuzla. And I was basically not expected to work with anyone above him, because that's the way the military hierarchy works - in the United Nations as well - you negotiate with and operate with and receive guidelines from and submit reports to and so on. I'm sure you're aware that I repeatedly interacted with the chief of staff immediately above Tuzla, General Nikolai, because we knew each other personally. And second, it's easier to arrange things quickly in your own language and to make things clear, knowing that you're skipping a level, the Tuzla level, but either simultaneously or retrospectively informing Tuzla. So basically, I was only required to interact with Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, we're going to get to the chain of command. I just wanted to know who you had to speak with so they could negotiate the release of your men. And if I understand your answer, you just went as high as Tuzla. You didn't bypass Tuzla to go to General Nikolai on this occasion. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: No, I didn't bypass it. Of course some -- what happened was that where the commander in Tuzla or his deputy, when they were not present, then you skip a step and you interact with the level above.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: On this occasion, did you interact with General Nikolai, who I believe was in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: No. I believe - and this was taking place in January - I was in touch with Tuzla to bring the matter to their attention there. I may have done this by phone. I may have spoken with CVO [as interpreted]. But I can only remember having interacted and communicated with Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you contact the Dutch Ministry of Defence to let them know that at least some of their men who had been sent there for peacekeeping purposes were actually being held hostage by the people they were supposed to be protecting?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: Yes. But the reports, as I did them for communication purposes, was all done through the channel of hierarchy with faxed copies to what we call the royal army crisis staff in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So you were just keeping them informed, as opposed to seeking guidance from those authorities?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: I kept them informed. Requesting aid is no use because it was an UN operation. And one of the countries applying the troops has no input to the ongoing operation at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Are you suggesting that the Dutch government would not have intervened to protect the hundred men that were being held hostage? Is that what you are suggesting? They would just leave it up to the UN to decide their fate?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: I think you should ask that question to somebody else. That undoubtedly would have happened in -- it happened in NATO situations as well. But that happens at an entirely different level. We're talking about an UN operation here, and let's not confuse two things. We're not talking about a country supplying troops that may or may not be able to influence an ongoing UN operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, one of the reasons, as I understand your previous answer, for your men being held hostage or being taken hostage in this area called the Bandera triangle was because you were trying to set up a reconnaissance post. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And would it -- could you please describe to us what is a reconnaissance post. I mean, I have the impression that it's there to collect information, to observe, to see if the Muslim army, for instance, is militarising in that area, helicopters flying in, people going in and out of the enclave. Would I be correct in that?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: That's right. I just referred to an old arrangement and an old observation post in the Bandera triangle at the edge of the border of the enclave. Based on the information available to us, I decided to include that observation post in some way within the belt of observation posts. But that didn't work out the way we wanted it to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please show us a map to indicate where this area is located in the safe area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So that we could have our directions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. With the Court's indulgence I was going to ask a couple more questions to lay the groundwork, but if that would be helpful right now I'll get to the map. I have it right here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I could show you what has been marked and what has come into evidence as P16.1. if you could just look at this. First of all, could you please tell us whether you identify with you -- whether you recognise what's on this map. Wonderful. Do you recognise it, sir?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: Yes, it does appear familiar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And what does it appear to be?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: This is a map depicting the boundaries of the safe area Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: And it indicates the observation posts that we set up at a later stage. I mean, this was not the case when I took over the area of DutchBat II, because this reflects more observation posts than were there when we took over the area. There's a reason that I may get into later on. The Bandera triangle is at the left around the Bravo observation post. That's what we call the Bandera triangle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Could you please point it out, sir, for us.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: [Witness complies].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In fact, why don't you just mark that so we know what precise area you had no access during the period that you were supposed to be patrolling that area.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: You'll find it in my book as one of the annexes; it's described very clearly there as to the coordinates where we were and were not enter. I could draw a line, but not a specific line as it's stated in my book.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I have your book handy -- you have it, too. If you want to look at your book as a reference. We're not looking at specific coordinates, but if you could keep it in scale so we have some sort of indication of the area of inaccessibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Perhaps if I could ask the monitor be darkened a little bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: In fact we do have a map that comes from DutchBat. It's on our exhibit list. If counsel wants to use that, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's fine, that's wonderful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Which means that you're allowed. So you're going to use this map?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Certainly, as long as it has that whole area they couldn't access to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Karremans.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And I believe it corresponds to the map which is showing the debriefing report Mr. Karnavas has quoted a couple of times.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Perhaps we can look at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now -- all right. So this is -- yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: [Witness complies].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So that's the Bandera triangle. Now, as I understand it you were -- your men were held hostage just about the time that you arrived -- DutchBat III arrived in Srebrenica. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: No, that's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, how long had you been there?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: We had been there for several weeks. The transfer of DutchBat II to DutchBat III had already taken place. In other words, I was already responsible for the area and the assignments carried out there. That's why I'm referring to the end of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: When did you arrive?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: Early January.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So within less than a month?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: Well, we discussed it -- well, imagine this: We arrived in the area that we would take over from the previous commander. There's an overlap period. So a battalion commander and a company commander arrived there first, in the first stroke -- at the first stage, and they had the most time to take command over from the predecessor who leaves at the last stage. So they have as long as possible to exchange information and to see --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Karremans, I don't mean to interrupt you and I apologise, but it was a very short question and I would like to get you back to Spain by tomorrow afternoon or evening or the next day as opposed to still being here on Monday. So I'm going to try to ask you to keep your answers as concise as possible. My question was: You were there less than a month before your men were held hostage; right?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And as a result of this incident, could you please describe to us the relationship thereafter between DutchBat and the Muslim army commanders, because I understand there were several of them in Srebrenica at that time - and correct me if I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: I can't answer that. You need to ask the local commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You mean that you had no dealings with the local commanders while you were there?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: Well, I was in touch with them and they're the ones you should ask who did I have contact with, who did I deal with and how did the relations evolve before, during, and after the hostage taking.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Where were the helicopter flights coming in to? Where were they landing, inside or outside the Bandera triangle?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: I did not see any helicopter flights, so I can't tell you that. But based on the information I received, from outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. When you say "outside," so are you saying it's outside the enclave that you were getting information about helicopter flights into the enclave. Is that what you're telling me?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: No. Our own reconnaissance posts told us that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: When you say your "own," is that DutchBat or UN? Because I understand there were UN military observers there as well.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: DutchBat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So your own soldiers, the ones that were there that were under you, were informing you of helicopter flights. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: No. They informed me that they -- that the sounds of helicopters had been heard; not where they landed, not what the intention was, whether the helicopters were loading or unloading. They only told us that helicopter sounds were heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: How frequently were these helicopter sounds?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Were there any -- were these helicopters being shot at?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: By us?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm not saying by you. I would have asked the question: Were you shooting down any helicopters or did you shoot at. Do you know whether the helicopters were shot at by either the Muslims or the Serbs? I don't know. I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know whether any helicopters had crashed?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: At one stage I believe one crashed, because we took care of somebody at the infirmary who was probably in one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, if he was in the infirmary and he was being taken care of, I take it as part of your mission to demilitarise this area you interrogated him, questioned him. I'm not suggesting something like what we're seeing in Iraq today, but you did question him, did you?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: No. It's not a matter of interrogation. It was one of the people in charge of the ABiH who required mild treatment at the centre or bandaging, and he told us something about the helicopter crash. And he said that many people had been killed there, in that. He not -- of course, not him. And in that situation, there's no point to interrogate somebody as might be happening today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, obviously you -- well, first of all did he tell you whether the crash took place inside or outside the enclave?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: Outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I take it you didn't venture out to see -- you didn't have your men go out of the enclave to see what might have happened.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: Under the mandate, we were not authorised to cross the border of the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did this gentleman who was -- when you say "ABiH," we're talking about he was military. Correct? Right?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: He was an officer, was he not?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you ask him whether that helicopter by chance was carrying arms into the enclave?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: No, no arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Are you saying that no arms were on the helicopter, or you didn't ask whether arms were on the helicopter, which of the two?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: Neither.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, if you didn't go to the crash site, you weren't on the helicopter, my question is: How do you know, then, that there were no arms on this helicopter unless you were told by someone and you took that person at their word? So who was it that told you, so at least we know whether we can take his word or not?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: I'm talking about Ramiz, the then-commander of the ABiH under Naser Oric, who was no longer there since April. And any conversation I heard that the helicopter moved personnel, particularly medical personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's what -- okay. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: And no arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. That's what this commander of the army told you; correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I take it you believed him.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Had you ever been misled by them before, not this individual but by the commanders of the Bosnian Muslim army inside the enclave?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: Misled is not the right word. But one didn't always get the right information that we wanted to have. Sometimes they beat around the bush. Sometimes information was held back, whereas we knew it existed, and then we used to say so in the talks. And then we saw them blushing. That applied to both sides. Usually the communication was open.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you mention Naser Oric. Did you get a briefing with respect to this particular individual, Naser Oric, before you got to -- took up your mission? Who he was, his adventures, his...

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And could you please tell us what exactly did they tell you about Mr. Oric.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: At the risk of -- Talking about Mr. Oric, Mr. Oric was written about in various books, including mine and so you can check it. During the period from January until the time I went on leave, I knew him and I experienced him to be a strong military leader who believed in what he did and was supported by most people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: A lot has been said about him in addition, truths and half truths, whatever one wishes to believe. And I do not really wish to deal with that because I cannot endorse it. I can only say what I think of it and how we dealt with each other during negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, since we're on the gentleman, I thought maybe we could speak a little bit about him because it might become relevant later on in our discussions here today. Again, going back to the book "Endgame." If I could put on the ELMO page 216. And again, this is for identification purposes D208. So if we could put on page 216. And I'll just read it. You can follow along. It says here: "Oric's men did commit atrocities, but how many is unclear. He was cavalier enough to show a video of a burned-down Serb village and headless Serb corpses to foreign journalists visits the enclave in February 1994." And there's a footnote to that. And then it goes on. "Several Muslims and Dutch peacekeepers reported seeing a photo of Oric standing over a Serb corpse in the ruins of a village." And then if I go to footnote number 42, and that would be found on page 419 of the book. It states: "The account was heard by so many different Muslim and Dutch sources that it was judged to be credible." My question to you, sir, is: Either before going to Srebrenica or while you were in Srebrenica, had you heard that Naser Oric was committing these sorts of atrocities, atrocities which we see on television now happening in Iraqi, where the whole world is up in arms about beheading of people. Were you ever informed of that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just entirely proper. I think we heard Iraq three times today. I don't see the relevancy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Beheading, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think there's no need to mention Iraq in these proceedings, which gives people a wrong impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I merely pointed it out because of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I know. Just ask your question there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. I thought it put some relevance to it, but very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Were you told that Mr. Oric was beheading Serbs and then displaying them as trophy cases?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And did you hear about that?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So it would appear, would it not, that at least while you were there you had learned that he was a war criminal?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, help me out here. Do you think it's appropriate for someone to be -- who is a military commander to either give orders to or to actually be himself -- the commander, that is -- behead civilians?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I think it's really an artificial discussion. Let me remind of what the witness said before. He said: "I've heard that but I don't really want to talk about it because I can only base my observation on what I've seen myself and I wrote it in my book." So it would be more appropriate to talk about Mr. Karreman's book, rather than what somebody else wrote.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may briefly respond. First of all, Naser Oric was running this show up until a point and then his other commanders were running the show. We will go through testimony where while Mr. Karremans was there to demilitarise, there were several incidents, especially in June, where soldiers were going out and committing atrocities against the Serbs and then running back into the enclave for protection under the UN blue helmets. Obviously he -- the gentleman had a mandate. I would like to know whether he was carrying out his mandate. If he knew the person was a war criminal or committing war crimes, what, if anything, he or his predecessors, his superiors, did about it, did anything about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, first of all I have to say that Mr. Oric is the accused in another case in this Tribunal, not in our case. Secondly, from the previous proceedings we learned that there is some evidence that Muslim troops attacked Serbs outside the safe areas. I don't think there is any disputes on that issue. But as I reminded you yesterday, we have to be very concentrated on the subject matter of our case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour. I'm like a laser beam on this one. Maybe it's not heading in the direction that -- maybe we have different directions but it's -- very well, Your Honour, I take your point. I will move on and try to cover the point in some other way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Let me ask you about whether you knew at that point in time about any activity of the Muslim army going out and committing atrocities or going out and actually engaging in military activity. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And I just want to be very clear on that, so help me out. During the entire time while you were there as the commander of the DutchBat, you never heard of any activities by the Muslim army going out and engaging in any activities. Is that what you're telling me? I just want to be clear on this.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: I won't talk about war criminals or whatever. I only talk about facts and figures. Observation posts have noted that from time to time Muslim fighters left the enclave and returned the same night. Sometimes one could hear fire exchanges taking place outside the enclave, and usually one or two days later one was informed by the -- one was informed by the other party that something had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's all you heard? You didn't hear any --

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: During the night you can only hear things; you can't see much. And you can only see as far as the eye reaches. And no one accompanied the people outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Did the Muslim soldiers ever impersonate themselves as DutchBat or UN soldiers with blue helmets shooting at the Serbs in order to attract fire?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: No, not that I know of.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You never heard of that while you were there.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And do you know whether the Muslims were digging trenches in front of the post?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: No, not in front of the post but between the posts. In areas where the visibility from an observation post was less, the ABiH have dug trenches.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And what was the purpose for putting the trenches over there so close to the observation post?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: No, not so close, in between. It is an area with a border of 50 kilometres with, initially, a small number of observation posts. So in brief, there were long stretches which could not be monitored, especially during the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: While you were there, what were your relations -- what were your relations with UNMO, the UN military observers? Were they passing on any information to you or were you just relying on your own people?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: Both. Meetings took place in which UNMOs took part, but UNMO is a different organisation. I was not their commander. At best, I had to offer them protection when necessary, and that was what was done at the end. They are not obliged to share information with the unit in the specific area. Of course this depends on the personal relationship with the commander of the UNMO team in order to obtain information anyhow.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So my question was: Were you receiving information from them? Did you have good relations with them? One UN group with another UN group, UNMO with UNPROFOR, the DutchBat, however you want to term yourself.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And I take it they were telling you about the activities of the Muslim fighters going out and trying to provoke the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: No. I explained at length that it is not possible when you do not go outside your area, because that was not part of the mandate. So that makes you dependent on the observations of other bodies. That could be the UN military-observer mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let me just be more concrete. Were the Muslim fighters, the army that was inside the enclave, were they going out, committing atrocities or engaging in military activity in order to provoke the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: As far as I recall the witness has been asked that before and I think he answered he heard it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We could go back to the transcript and to see; this question has been asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I didn't ask the question about provocation, Your Honour. I asked whether there were -- that's why the difference in the question. Whether they were going out provoking, in other words trying to engage the Serbs into responding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, as for the purpose of those attacks, I believe only those engaged in that type of activity could answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I would like to know, Your Honour, whether Mr. Karremans saw that as a -- saw those acts as acts of provocation. If I may be permitted to ask that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, you may put this question, but bear in mind that that is a speculative question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I will bear that in mind, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Would you like that answer that question, Mr. Karremans?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: No, it is a speculative question. I won't answer that.
