The second thing I want to say is that during the final period and also during the fall of Gorazde, the VRS or the BSA often made use of those articles which had been stolen and so on. I am referring to the robbery at OP Echo. They had a few minutes, because they were under fire, to leave the observation post. They had to leave behind most of their personal belongings, of course which clothes were part of but it also included arms, ammunition, and communication material. All of that was taken away. Later possibly it was used. But the same happened also in the Gorazde area where the French and the British suddenly had to leave observation posts. So in short, it is possible and possibly it happened on both parts, as it says under 4.13, quite close to an observation post. But shooting while wearing these clothes, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, it didn't happen? No, you're not aware of it? Which of the two?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: I should have been aware if disguised ABiH personnel were shooting at the VRS near observation posts. The latter I know, as I said this morning, but the latter wearing a disguise, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I just want to be clear that I understand you. You're not suggesting is that it wasn't happening; what you're suggesting -- what you're telling us is you were not aware of this activity.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So you're not necessarily challenging what is in the debriefing.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. If we could move on to another area. I think we covered that fairly nicely. I want to talk a little bit about the humanitarian situation or the situation in the enclave. And if you could be -- I understand there came a point in time when there was a shortage of food and fuel in the enclave. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: Everything a military man needs to perform his military duty was not present there and was intentionally kept behind. At General Mladic's staff, they knew exactly what our applications were and what our needs were with regard to fuel, food, ammunition, communication materials, and bandaging and drugs. And for a long period, none of that all ever arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Is there a particular reason, in your opinion, why it did not arrive?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: I think you should put that question to somebody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, we spent a lot of time so far describing the situation that you were there -- while you were there. You've informed us that it wasn't demilitarised. In fact, it became more militarised. You've told us, or at least we covered, the fact that there was increased activity as far as military action outside the enclave. And it would appear from NIOD it wasn't for food but rather, these were military objectives. I asked you earlier about the perception of the Serbs -- of the VRS, that perhaps they may perceive or they may have perceived that you were giving aid and comfort to the very same soldiers that you were supposed to demilitarise. Do you think that might have been perhaps a reason why they were restricting the aid to the enclave? Could that be a possibility?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: No. You are using the word "perhaps," so therefore I can answer this. I know some explanations, but all of that was with hindsight. The explanations -- I may have discussed at the time with Franken about why could they possibly do it, about all of that I can say only one thing, namely that it wasn't smart for them to do so. Because of this and because of restricting all means that you need to keep running a large unit with a specific duty is that in the end they succeeded in preventing us from doing our duty. So in that respect you have to say in conclusion that in that respect only one side is to blame.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: I mean to say, if I may say some more --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: Consciously and intentiously [as interpreted], materials were held from us in order to prevent us from doing our work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Perhaps we could go back to the NIOD report if you could help us out with that one. Again for identification purposes as D210. I'm going to point you to part 3, chapter 1, section 14. Incidentally, the side that you indicated was to blame - I take it you're -- that's the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: Across the board and in a great many cases, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Across the board. So the Muslim side was not to blame at all in spite of the activities that we spoke of. You said across the board; that's why I'm going that route.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: I mean if the VRS or the BSA had allowed the DutchBat, the Dutch Battalion, to normally do its job - that means that instead of doing -- patrolling on foot, doing these by vehicle - that we could have sent out larger patrols more frequently, thereby, in fact, the BSA from a military point of view has inversed [as interpreted] the situation with the consequence that we could do less and the ABiH could afford to do more. In other words, they finally shot themselves in the foot. Of course, the ABiH is also to blame somewhat. I referred this morning to the provocative behaviour such as digging trenches and openly running around with arms after the demilitarisation period and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. What about the converse? Had DutchBat done its job - the UN, I don't want to blame the DutchBat - but had the UN done its job and had Srebrenica been demilitarised as it had been agreed upon, do you think perhaps it would never have been attacked? There would have been no need.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: This is an if question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I'll back it up afterwards.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: I can't answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Did you have a conversation with General Mladic at any point in time with respect to that?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: The very last time just before the departure of the battalion from the enclave, I asked him this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. And the answer that you got was, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: It was not really clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. It wasn't really clear. All right. Well, we'll get to that at some point. But let me go back to the NIOD report. If there's --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What's the objection? Mr. McCloskey, I seem some commotion going on. I don't see the problem. I'm going to get to it. I will put my case to the witness, Your Honour. They need not worry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The point is if there is an issue which can be dealt with right now, I think it should be done for the sake of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I think that I'm going to move at my pace, Your Honour. And we will get to it, because he indicated the last time he saw General Mladic - and as we will find out it was after the fall of Srebrenica - so chronologically speaking we're going to get to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Up to now we have many issues that we need to come back. I just want to remind you about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just one second, Your Honour. There's so many documents around. If I could have the Court's indulgence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Maybe we can look at your book, page 239. It's in Dutch, and I can put it on the ELMO, although there are few of us - the usher being one - who could read it. But I believe there is a reference in your book on page 239 about the last meeting in Fontana with Mladic where you asked him whether the enclave would still exist if the ABiH had not been carrying out the attacks, and that Mladic said yes. Is that on that page, by any chance?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Oh, okay. So there -- in your book there's no equivocation.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: [In English] It's yes, for what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, I appreciate that, and I guess that Mr. Waespi got his answer. There's no need to go back to that point. Now, if I could go back to where I was before the objection, the NIOD report, part 3, chapter 1, section 14; again, D210 for identification. I would like to show you page 1 and 2. If we go down to the last two paragraphs, and we're going to go on to the next page as well. It states here: "Early June: Smith arrived at a new estimate of the objectives of the warring factions." Okay. And we see at the top of the page we're talking about the spring of 1995, and that would be June of 1995. So there's no dilemma as to the date or period. "Objective of the VRS with regard to UNPROFOR was to neutralise it by regulating or denying reapply, in particular for fuel. That would affect UNPROFOR's power to such an extent that the safe-area concept would be emasculated after which the VRS could freely attack the opponents. From a military viewpoint, the objective of the VRS would to keep existing pressure on the enclaves to be able to reduce their size. The underlying objective was to release manpower for operations around Sarajevo, because to the VRS, Sarajevo maintained the centre of the activities. Yet Smith did not think the risk of offensive operations to take all of the eastern enclaves particularly great at the moment. Its political implications, the negative publicity and a lack of infantry made it unlikely, according to Smith. Rather, the VRS tactics seemed to aim at besieging the ABiH troops in the enclaves to exhaust them, and to force them to surrender." Then it goes on and says: "Smith was convinced that the VRS was counting on it that actions against the enclaves would not invoke a response from NATO, therefore the VRS would continue shelling military targets within the enclave. The ABiH in the enclaves were going to lose ground. The defenders would gradually run out of ammunition and would have to find refuge in more densely populated areas. Conversely, Smith thought that the Bosnian Muslims would do anything to get UNPROFOR, NATO and the international community on their side. Smith expected that the ABiH would be going to use UNPROFOR as a protective shield. The result would be that the VRS could be shooting at UNPROFOR as a deterrence. That way, the ABiH would try to drag UNPROFOR into the conflict. In this scenario, the safety of the UN soldiers was not directly at risk, but casually through crossfire was possible." So my question now, Mr. Karremans, is: Do you agree or disagree with this passage from the NIOD report?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now -- yes, it's a ten-time compound question. What he asked is now basically Mr. Karremans to comment on about five, six different points Mr. Smith made at some time, and we don't even know whether -- we don't have the source whether it was Mr. Smith who said. I think it's improper to ask Mr. Karremans to make a comment on that, unless he has talked with Mr. Smith about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, here we are talking about the facts, so I just want the witness to see whether the facts are true or not, whether he knows something about what's written here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I could go to the first paragraph, because we're talking about supplies now coming in and out of the enclave. And the first part talks about the objectives of the VRS not allowing the resupplying. Getting back to what I was saying earlier, do you know why the VRS was not allowing all of the supplies to come into the enclave?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, I believe you testified at the Rule 61 hearing that - if I could put my hand on it - that no convoys, after a certain point, no convoys at all were coming in, either for DutchBat or UNHCR. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And just so my learned colleagues know exactly what I'm referring to, let me read a portion of your testimony, and we'll take it from there. This would be found on page 636, line 2. I'll start with actually line 1. "That could explain something on the circumstances up to 6 July. Those, let us say miserable circumstances in April, May, June were caused, what I said yesterday, by refusing the incoming convoys, either by the battalion or by UNHCR, for the refugees. Thus, we had to do with a strangulation of the entire -- of the enclave or so to call an isolation, a total blockade." Do you recall making that statement, sir?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: Yes, I made that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And do you --

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: I don't remember -- I said this. It's written there. I don't remember saying why. At best after a number of suggestions about why they should do that, but we don't want to respond to reactions. The fact is that during a prolonged period but also the population during a prolonged period have been strangled and were cut off from everything a population and a unit need in human terms. The fact that this is connected with what you were referring to in the first instance, namely a higher objective of the VRS, or possibly a higher objective - and I'm referring to Sarajevo - attacks by the ABiH, to the extent I could judge at that time is a separate thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But that wasn't my question, but thank you. I think that is a useful answer anyway. But I just want to make sure that you stand by your response that there were no incoming convoys, either for the battalion or by UNHCR for the refugees.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. Now, do you recall the yellow bridge that's separated --

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In fact, there was a rather colourful character there by the name of Jovo who was sort of the komandir. Do you recall that -- do you recall that gentleman? He spoke Russian.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, in fact we -- he was here and he testified. And while he was here, he was shown several documents. And I thought I would take this opportunity to share them with you and perhaps you may comment on them. I'm going to start with --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And if the usher could just kind of keep himself strategically there so he doesn't have to walk back and forth too much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we go to D177, Defence Exhibit 177. If you look at that. And it's dated May 19, 1995. It would appear that we have a convoy going into Srebrenica, do we not?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: [In English] Are you still waiting for my answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think this question should be put to the representatives of the units who worked in my area, because they may have a different opinion about the number of convoys that entered the area in the final period, if I -- if you understand what I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, just for --

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: May I add something?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Please. Please do.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: Things tended to disappear on the way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You mean sort of in this way?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And by that I mean theft. Now --

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: Much was handed in also in terms of Dutch convoys which entered the area, and it had to be paid for in terms of fuel, in terms of money, and in means of goods.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But -- and I don't want to go through all these documents unless we have to, and I was going to refer just for the record to D173, 174, 175, and of course 177. If we look at all these documents which were brought in through Jovo, that particular individual who was the komandir at the yellow bridge, his testimony was - and it would appear that the documentation reflects - that humanitarian aid was indeed coming in, which is remarkably different from your testimony under oath back in July 1996 where you said after a certain point there -- you said, and I read again, that: "Let us say, miserable circumstances in April, May, and June were caused, what I said yesterday, by refusing the incoming convoys, either by the battalion or by UNHCR for the refugees." And if we look at other material, it would appear that April -- I think it's April 26th is the date when convoys supposedly no longer came in to Srebrenica. So here we have documents dating -- showing that they came. You're saying nothing came in. What are we to make of this? Who's right? Who's wrong?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: I stick to my point of view. I don't know these documents. I don't know their content. I stick to my point of view based on my own observations and the observations of my UNHCR representatives and the battalion and people from the population that nothing or hardly anything came in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, now you're switching it to hardly. You're giving yourself some room. What if I were to say - and we can go through this in great detail - but what if I were to say in my hands I have portions of the NIOD report from part 3, chapter 4 in sections 2, sections 3, sections 9, all of which reflect that convoys and humanitarian aid, albeit restricted, was coming into the enclave? And if you want, I can go through them in great detail; it's up to you.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: No, you don't have to go into detail. I don't know who wrote these documents; I don't know where the information came from. I gave you what I know and what I noted in discussions, hearing that nothing came in. And you say that I alleviated by saying hardly. I can say it more strictly. Next to nothing came in. If these documents say that there was sufficient supply arriving, then I doubt the contents of these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just one moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, maybe we could just look at one of these. And if I could refer you to part 3, chapter 4, section 2. And again this would be D210 for identification, and we'll be looking at page 3. Now, this was a portion, I believe, that might have been read when Jovo was here. I'm going to read from the bottom of the page, last paragraph, and the top of the next page. It says here: "In the meantime, in the meantime, the ABiH in Sarajevo -- I mean in Srebrenica, I apologise, in Srebrenica appeared to be taking good care of itself. In May, the ABiH separated approximately 40 tonnes of goods from UNHCR aid that had reached the enclave from the aid to the population." And now we're talking about May. We're talking about 40 tonnes of goods from the UNHCR. "This implied a considerable risk. If the Bosnian Serbs were to find out the aid to the population could be limited even further." So we don't have what you indicated, "next to nothing," but it seems that some aid or a considerable amount actually is coming in. It goes on to say: "It was also noteworthy that the chief of the defence sector in the enclave, Professor Suljo Hasanovic, reported from the enclave to the defence secretariat of the Ministry of Defence of the Tuzla canton that the ABiH had also received some food from DutchBat. For the same reason, if the Bosnian Serbs were to intercept this message traffic - which was not unlikely - and irrespective of whether this message was true, it could have given the VRS an additional reason" to tighten "the thumbscrews on DutchBat." Now, it would appear here from the NIOD report from the Dutch government that, one, 40 tonnes was being stolen, and I'll use that word, by the ABiH from UNHCR aid to the people, to the refugees. So this was not Serbs steeling it but rather Muslim fighters. And also it seems that this professor here reported that DutchBat had given food to the ABiH. Do you have an opinion regarding this?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: [In English] Sure, I have an opinion. [Interpretation] I don't know about over 40 tonnes, because 40 tonnes is an awful lot of food. We discussed this morning that parts of incoming food aid did go to the ABiH. Food that the battalion provided was discussed in advance by Mr. Franken and myself because during a period with a certain surplus of some types of food, we were unable to refrigerate it because we -- it didn't have any diesel. So we gave parts of the food away to -- at the outside. But we didn't -- we said we can't give it to one side and not to the other side. It was never the idea for leftovers of food supplies for the battalion, for the reasons I just mentioned, to end up with the ABiH. The food that was given away was for the population. The population suffered the most, not for the combating parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we could turn to page 5 and just check the footnote. This is footnote 18 to that section. It may help us out here a little bit. And footnote 18 notes that this information or some of it at least. It says: "ICTY," that's this place here, "IT-98-33," a reference to a case, D55. Then it states, "Chief of the defence sector, Professor Suljo Hasanovic to the Defence ministry Tuzla defence secretariat, department Srebrenica municipality, 05/06/95, number 03-49-5/95." And then there is a list and the list shows: "2.500 kilograms of four, 596 kgs of sugar, 1423 litres of cooking oil, 619 kgs of salt, 5.000 kgs of beans, 17.020 of cold cuts, 100 kgs of powdered milk, 62 kgs of juice, 7.780 tins of fish, 1290 kgs of cauliflower, 90 kgs of kale, 150 kgs of carrots, 240 kgs of green beans, 171 litres of heating oil, and one litre of motor oil. So it's a rather detailed list of items.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'm sorry Mr. Karremans can give an explanation, but it would have been proper to dig up this exhibit, since it is a Defence exhibit --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's a footnote.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I don't understand the objection. Maybe I'm tired. I don't know what it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: The problem is we don't have that document as well as the footnote. We don't know where it comes from. That's the problem. Maybe you could give more indications on this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I apologise if we haven't provided copies. I'll apologise in advance. Normally this is not what we do. This is from the NIOD report and we can make copies -- it's on the Internet. That's where we pulled it out, but it is from the NIOD report. This particular section, as I understand, was already discussed when a previous witness was here. This is from chapter 4 -- part 3, chapter 4, section 2 of the NIOD report, and that's a report that was prepared by the Dutch government. It's about 8.000 pages. I've been contemplating to bring the whole report in or whether to just streamline it as I'm doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Now, the case that you mentioned, is that Krstic case?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Oh, that particular case? I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm told that it is. I am told that it is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I believe that there is an identification number --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: On that case, you know. Could you please find that document if possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I can. I can. But perhaps my learned colleagues would know it off the top of their head.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: It is certainly the Krstic case and all exhibits of the Krstic case have been disclosed to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So what's the problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: This is the examination-in-chief, Mr. Karnavas, and you're supposed to give us the exhibits or whatever you are putting to the witness in advance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: But you may proceed. Maybe tomorrow morning we could get the related documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: But you can move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Things do fall through the cracks. I apologise to my learned colleagues. I trust they've had all the other portions of the NIOD report that I've been reading from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, there's thousands of documents of this case. If you don't give them the number or the name of the document, how could they know which document are they going to need? Although we see several trolleys of documents there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Getting back to the question. It would appear, would it not, sir, that from this rather detailed list - from a -- what would appear to be a Prosecution witness, might I add - that food was coming in and food was taken by the ABiH. But also food was given to ABiH by the DutchBat --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'm not sure why Mr. Karnavas uses Prosecution witness perhaps to enhance the credibility of what he's saying, but there was no Prosecution like that in the Krstic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think this issue was mentioned from that report. You just quote the report and put your question to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: My advice is try to avoid any unnecessary mentioning of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm doing my best, Your Honour. I think I'm doing fairly well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Getting back to my question and I'll ask it again. It would appear from reading the NIOD report that a fairly large quantity of food, foodstuff that came into the enclave was taken by the ABiH or stolen, but also that the DutchBat had been giving foodstuff to the ABiH. That's what the NIOD, the Dutch government, is stating. So would you please give us your opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I believe it has been asked and answered many times and we can go on forever on this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, Your Honour, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think at the beginning this question was asked but the context is a little bit of difference. So you may proceed. Witness, you may answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. What you just heard seems probable, gigantic quantities. But I would recommend that in the months April, May, June, early July, an account of what actually arrived for a population 40 to 50.000, because what you have here in front of you can't even feed 5.000 people properly for a week. This is just a drop in the bucket. And I get the impression that matters are being discussed behind my back or presented or referred to that I have not seen before because you're producing all kinds of documents. I can't answer your question. All I can say is I suggest that you check the entire supplies of the population from a humanitarian perspective and see exactly what arrived because I seriously doubt this information. Second, the idea that the battalion received surplus food is something I explained and I told you why as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But if we were to look at that particular document that I just showed you, does it not contradict your testimony under oath back in 1996 where you said no convoys were coming in, either for DutchBat or UNHCR? It does -- would you concede that point at least?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: Maybe I said none too explicitly. I said none or hardly any just now, and I'm inclined to say none because this is a load of two or three or four vehicles, and that's just a drop in the bucket. And I'll correct my statement: Hardly anything arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, I guess we'll have to go to one more of these. If I can get the assistance of the usher. I want to go to part 3, chapter 4, section 9, and again this would be D210. And if we could start with page 4. Just for the sake of time, I just want to go through this rather quickly. Page 4 if we look at in the middle of the page it says: "The convoy left Belgrade on the 17th of June, about 13 kilometres before Srebrenica on the Bosnian Serb territory, it was stopped because of an unsafe situation." And then it goes on. The next paragraph it says: "The convoy did indeed return to Zvornik and stayed there overnight. The VRS arranged a guard and shared their rations with the convoy supervisors. Although safety could still not be guaranteed, no prohibition on continuing was forthcoming." Then the next paragraph, the last paragraph of the page. "At yellow bridge, the VRS both on the outward and return journey carefully checked the quantity of fuel in the vehicle's tanks. The VRS soldiers appeared friendly, but the convoy leader could not say that about DutchBat. The DutchBat soldiers were instructed to check the vehicles, which was done conscientiously." And in fact there's a reference there about Major Franken. Now, if we go down to the middle of the page, this would be page 5, part 3, chapter 4, section 9. It says: "On 20 June, another UNHCR convoy arrived in the enclave, this time with 56 tonnes of sugar, beans, salt, fish, flour, soap, powdered milk, and biscuits. Again, DutchBat searched the convoy more thoroughly than the VRS had done. What is more, the VRS had first tapped some fuel from each tank until 100 to 150 litres remained. According to the UNMO present on the site, the convoy commander now again objected to the check by DutchBat, and informed his headquarters. The result was that a convoy planned for the next day would be cancelled unless DutchBat changed the procedure. UNHCR had no objection to a check of the identity papers on the entering the enclave, but the most logical place for the load was the unloading point in Srebrenica itself." And then it goes on. It appears from the NIOD report, the report prepared by the Dutch government, that not only convoys were coming in, the DutchBat were inspecting those convoys and in fact it would appear that the DutchBat were irritating UNMO in the manner in which they were being checked. Were you aware of that, sir, you being the commander of the DutchBat at the time?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: I don't know the source of this statement by the NIOD. The NIOD interviewed many, many different people at all sides. I do know that the VRS or the BSA responded to allowing convoys to enter, both at the start with the staff and throughout the period in later no longer. Convoys containing food and other products such as fuel and the like, they would perform a check, a second check, a third check. And as I says here, occasionally they would take something away along route. The account about convoys being attacked en route by the ABiH outside the area that was under the battalion's responsibility is something that I cannot confirm. It may have been said; it may have been made up. But that unethical practices took place from the area where they entered the -- where the convoys entered until the date of Ipapa where the convoys entered the enclave, during -- along that stretch many things undoubtedly happened. And it might be advisable to consult the representative of the UNHCR whose name I've seen and to ask him exactly what happened with the convoys and the numbers and the way the staff were treated and the like.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: Second, I believe that checking -- the checks by DutchBat staff of the convoys was not so bad. We agreed that convoys, especially humanitarian-aid convoys, such as there were, would be accompanied, escorted from the entrance of the enclave, up to the city of Srebrenica, where the contents would be distributed for several reasons. You may not be able to imagine this, but 40.000 people with little or no food for weeks can do all kinds of things to get food along a stretch of a few kilometres. So that's what I agreed with the -- one of the people I agreed about this with was the UNHCR representative.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, we're not talking about the regular folks; we're talking about the ABiH, the Muslim army. And it appear they were well-fed and they certainly had fuel for their needs. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: I don't know where the ABiH obtained their fuel. I didn't have any, that's a well-known fact. And what is more -- then I might have been led down the wrong path about who the VRS is. But it wasn't the ABiH that removed fuel from the convoys.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, before I just move from that area, would you agree with me or perhaps you could share your opinion with us. If the ABiH was going out committing atrocities against civilians and if, as it would appear in these documents, the DutchBat was giving food to the ABiH, could one draw the conclusion that perhaps there was some aiding and abetting between DutchBat and the ABiH? I'm not saying that that was the case, but could someone draw that wrong conclusion?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: No. The conclusion is reached with people sitting around the table. It starts with a breakout of the ABiH for the wrong reasons or words to that effect. And the second suggestion presented would be to say that we fed the Muslim combatants or the ABiH so that they were able to fight with full stomachs. And I take issue, I disagree, with both statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Finally, you said that you had a loss of -- you had a shortage of fuel. I thought I just wanted to share this one part with you. This is from the NIOD report, part 2, chapter 8, section 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again for identification purposes, D210. If I could get this on the ELMO, page 5, I guess. Part 2, chapter 8, section 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It states here, again this is from the NIOD report in the middle of the page: "On 10 May 1995 DutchBat entered the state of superminimise, which meant that all lights were turned out (the dark ages). There was no more TV and hot water and neither were there any normal meals." And then it goes on. In the next paragraph it states "Paradoxically enough, the Serbs in Bratunac supplied diesel to the battalion so that DutchBat would continue to drive to Bratunac in a 4-tonner to buy beer." Do you know whether this was going on, you didn't have fuel to do patrolling, but the Serbs were giving you diesel so they could do beer runs into Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: No, I'm not really interested in beer anyway in this context. What is at issue here is the intent, the underlying intent, how we handled the diesel problem. I wrote about that at length in my book. I don't mean that people were almost killed to get it, but the way that a unit was stationed under UN authorities to perform an assignment and was under such pressure in part through a diesel shortage, that we had to impose a regime and observation posts and vehicle commanders for the compounds and regulate the use of diesel, at a certain point nobody drove. I didn't even command as the commander. The only vehicles driving were Red Cross vans in case of emergencies. And this story about 4 tonnes to Bratunac for BSA or VRS that Nikolic might have arranged, no. Up to a certain point there was an opportunity to do business in Bratunac where two men did that, and of course at a certain point that ended, too. And it all coincides with the early period that I mentioned. And then we said: Okay, we're going to discontinue this because we're not getting anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I know we're just about out of time but I want to go back to this point. Here it talks about the Serbs supplying the DutchBat with diesel to make beer runs into town. That would be about 10 kilometres, or 5 if you're from Potocari. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And with respect to the business that you talked about, and I think we had this when Major Franken or I believe he's lieutenant colonel now, there were some efforts, were there not, for there to be some trading between the Serbs and the Muslims in the enclave that Nikolic was arranging?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: Suggestions had been made during the early period that led us to check via a medium called Nikolic to see whether it would be possible to do business between the battalion unit and the people or a few businesses in Bratunac on the other hand. So that effort was made in the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And as I understand it, Nikolic was interested in the business because of his fondness for money, while the ABiH was not interested in having any business. And that's why the trading never took place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Nice question to finish today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That is the last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I said nice. It's improper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I don't think this question as you put it is proper, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You asked this witness to speculate. How could he know Nikolic was interested in business?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: He writes about it in his book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Because of his fondness of money. How could his witness know that? That's ridiculous.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's in his book, that's how I know. He knows that Nikolic was interested in money. And in fact, he has a rather unkind characterisation. It's on page 121.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I don't think this question is necessary. Please drop it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could just have a moment, not long, after the witness leaves, if I could address the Court briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In your book you did write about the trading issue.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS KARREMANS
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I think that's it for today and tomorrow we're going to pick up right around the events concerning Srebrenica, right around the 9th, 10th, more like the 10th, 11th so we all know where we're going to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Witness, I think you have to say here for another night and we'll continue the proceedings tomorrow. So during your stay here, you have to understand that you are under oath, so do not discuss the testimony or do not let anybody talk to you about your testimony. And I'll see you tomorrow and I wish you a good rest tonight. The usher will show you out of the room.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, I think we need the document D210, which is the NIOD report prepared by the Dutch government tomorrow morning. I hope you could furnish us with that document, since this document was extensively used in this proceeding, as well as the exhibit D55 in the Krstic case which you used, listing all those items.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And another thing is about this witness's book: "Who cares." If you are going to use certain parts of that book, it's better to have it translated into English so we could not be misled.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't want to get into the issue of resources. I think my Court has heard my story on that one. It was just since the gentleman was here he could read a portion for the record. I don't intend to introduce any part of that and since we have some very fine translators. But I take the point. As far as the NIOD portions, I take it the Court only wishes me to make copies of the portions we're referencing, not the 8.000 pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, the relevant parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: With respect also, Your Honour, and I don't mean to be disputatious at this point, but with respect to the footnote that I read, that was footnote 18 from the Krstic, obviously it was in the footnote. I don't have access to that material, so it's an impossible task, if I could use that word, since we talked about impossibility today at some point. So I don't think I can provide that information, though I can -- it's in the footnote, in the NIOD report, and I can certainly get it at some point. But by tomorrow morning, that's beyond a Herculean task.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Try your best. You may ask assistance from the other party or from the registrar. We cannot accept anything that only has a list. Maybe there's something more in that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We'll try.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just on that last point, that was a Defence Krstic exhibit and the Defence had been provided with all the Defence Krstic exhibits. We understand the problem and there's -- they got a lot of stuff, so do we. But we will assist them, though I know Ms. Tomanovic is very well organised. So perhaps if she needs our help, please let us know but I know they have that. In addition, I just wanted to point out what I -- is obvious, but Mr. Karremans was not called as a Prosecution witness. He is a Defence witness and he is clearly being impeached, which is fine. But, for example, the issue is not part of the Prosecution's case that all aid was cut off. I think the Court remembers the famous VRS documents where they wanted to restrict the aid. So this point that -- where Mr. Karremans said about no convoys, that can go to his credibility. But to take a Defence witness and to take his credibility down on -- when he hasn't been offered by the Prosecution to provide anything, really doesn't have a whole lot of relevance to anything. Now, had he testified about substantive matters in direct examination that caused -- that Mr. Karnavas wanted to attack, then his credibility is open at all levels. But to start him out by just attacking his credibility, it is really not proper adversarial process and it gives the strong appearance that Mr. Karremans is on trial. And perhaps I wouldn't have said anything except that as we could see the insinuation or the -- it wasn't -- it was more than an insinuation, that because DutchBat didn't have any diesel, their freezers didn't work, their food was going to go to waste, so they gave some food to the Muslims. That's what he said. And Mr. Karnavas suggested that by giving food to the Muslims he was participating in or assisting in the atrocities created by the Muslims. Not only is that six jumps ahead of rationality, but that will inflame the witness. It puts him unfairly on trial. I believe it's what the Court was referring to the other day when it spoke let's show respect to the witnesses. Then we went into the whole beer thing and Momir Nikolic, which again seemed to be taking us down into this gutter, which if we put this witness on as a Prosecution witness, there's a certain amount of fair game to that. But to put him on and then take him to the gutter, it seems gratuitous to me. And I just wanted to point that out. I don't think it is the proper way. And also the continual reading of document. In his own witness he can use it to refresh the recollection of the witness if he doesn't remember or to specifically impeach him on a point if he can be determined adverse. Long readings of a complicated ten-point thing and asking him to comment on it, it leaves the record very confused and will go on and on and on. So those would be my comments. I do appreciate Mr. Karnavas has not put the Prosecution in his sights today and we're very happy about that. And if Mr. Karremans is going to be put in his sights, fine. But if it can be put on a relevant issue where Mr. Karremans has done something to the case that's being brought forward. But those would be my points.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Briefly respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, very briefly. We are running out of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. First of all, Mr. Karremans did testify as a Prosecution witness back in 1996 and he made some comments. I don't know whether the Prosecution is going to go to those documents or not. Obviously I have some concerns. Also, the gentleman does seem to have a particular slant on the events, so I do need to make sure that we start with a proper foundation. And I believe he had indicated on several occasions one thing and then later on when shown documents at least he's come closer to where the document is or he has maintained his position. Secondly, I don't think I'm treating the gentleman unfairly. Even though I called him does not mean that I cannot, in a very gentle fashion as I have been doing, perhaps point him in the right direction or point him the errors of his ways. I don't think that's improper, and I've done this on many occasions. He's not exactly a neutral witness or a Defence witness in the classical sense, and that's the dilemma that I'm in. So I'm trying to do the best I can under the circumstances. And I do appreciate the Prosecution giving me some leeway. That has been noticed, although I'm a little disheartened by their recent remarks. It pains me to hear these sorts of things that somehow I'm being unfair and unkind to a witness. As far as putting him through the ringer and trying to embarrass him, that's not the intention. All of this is background information. It goes to the theory of the case. The Prosecution has repeatedly argued that this was an operation that ultimately had its designs to meet the six or seven points, that is to ethnically cleanse the area. And what I'm trying to demonstrate is that this is a far more complex picture and we can't just look at the surface of it. So that's all. Now, tomorrow we're going to go right into the heart of the matter and we're going to move along. And if I need to sort of correct him, I'm going to have to do that. I do it in a most gentle fashion. I think I'm being very mindful of our host, the Dutch government, who has been kind enough to assist us. And I want to commend them. I think they've done a marvelous job trying to bring out the truth in the Dutch report. It's a public document. If they felt comfortable and publishing it so the whole world can see it in a very transparent matter which should be done elsewhere, specifically in places of the world where issues are ongoing, I won't mention the place. In any event, I will be very gentle and streamline and I take Mr. McCloskey's comments to heart. I take them to heart. And I will do my utmost to abide within the good atmosphere that we have in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, thank you very much for your attitude. Well, I think this witness is important since he's an eyewitness to many events, and there are many publications nowadays on the Srebrenica massacres. But we have a witness, an eyewitness here. He could give some evidence with the probative value, and there's no doubt. Secondly, I would like to say that maybe, Mr. Karnavas, you are used to cross-examination, maybe not quite used to direct examination. And this is a witness called by you, and I don't see this witness as hostile to your case. He just tells you the truth. It is very helpful for the Judges, for this Bench, to know what was really happening on the spot. This is the main purpose. There is no difference between the Prosecution's case -- Prosecution's witness and the Defence witness in terms their testimony. Because the only purpose for them to come here is to help us, the Judges, to have a better understanding of the situation. But there is some differences between the direct examination and the cross-examination. I believe that Mr. Karnavas will understand that. The third point is that there are some questions which are really not proper. For instance, you couldn't blame the DutchBat as aiding and abetting for all those crimes. The best way is to put the facts there and let the Judges, the Bench, draw the conclusion. The witness is a military man; he is not a legal expert. Up to now, the Judges are starting the meaning of aiding and abetting this minute, so I don't think this witness could appreciate your question at all. And there is some implied meaning by your question to blame the DutchBat for some criminal activities, which is, if I could say, out of the scope, out of the scope. So lastly, I'm very glad to hear that tomorrow we'll come to the more substantial matters. And I only hope that tomorrow we could finish the testimony of this witness on time. This is all I could say for this witness. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just a housekeeping case. Your Honour, Mr. Karnavas and I have spoken of this one last 92 bis witness, and I went and I did read him over again. And unless the Court wants us to call him, at this point I can -- would be satisfied by not calling him. I think perhaps we'll go interview him and see if he has anything else to say that may be of relevance through another 92 bis comment. But at this point unless the Court wants us to cross-examine that witness, I'm fine not calling him. And I just wanted to mention that to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, could I regard it as an oral motion to withdraw your request for the cross-examination of that 92 bis witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Oh, thank you very much. But we have to inform the registrar as soon as possible because everything for the preparation is in process at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We can --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We can do that. We can do that, assuming that it's a done deal --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Assuming that this is -- that the Court makes a ruling, we can contact to put a halt to the process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So this request is granted by this Bench. Well, we are 20 minutes past the time allocated to us, so I would like to thank the interpreters and the court reporter and the other technicians to allow us to sit a little bit longer. I apologise for that, and I promise that tomorrow we'll finish on time. So the hearing for today is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 25th day of June, 2004, at 9.00 a.m.
